comments.author: @cacogenicist
comments.text:
I know the "AGI" goal post has moved quite a lot since the early aughts, but I think an AI system that warrants the label must feature continuous learning, either via an infinite context window, or continuous updating of the underlying model weights. 

These things are necessary for an AI agent to truly be a drop-in replacement for a white collar human employee. The systems need long-term memory, and a way to permanently integrate new information and skills. 

This just isn't a thing yet, and it doesn't look like it's going to be solved in the next few years. 

If these systems are AGI now, they're AGI that suffered catastrophic strokes or traumatic brain injuries.

comments.text: Next thing after reasoners and RL is probably a mixture of evolutionary approaches in the CoT (see alpha evolve, Darwin goedel mashine, absolute star…) and something like SEAL (self adapting language models) to update their model weights on the run. Also i think the  reinforcement learning needs to leave pure text space and into spatial and optical reasoning. Like having ai simulated worlds in which the multi model agents interact with one another (already done for RL in robotics, but not for LLMs. We probably need to bring together  the reinforcement reasoning training paradigm of LLMs together with the RL training paradigm of robots in one holistic multi modal model)

comments.text: Any mathematician will attest to the fact that math olympiads are challenging even at the national level. If any person or AI model at any level, is able to consistently solve these independently within the set limits and conditions, then that is a truly impressive ability. What it does have is the sledge-hammer approach of iteration and recursion, mass computation which could work for certain types of problems. In short, I'm not completely convinced. How much compute was used? What kind of problems were they trained on? How exactly is mathematical expressions and notations being translated into llm-friendly form. How many attempts did they have. Isn't it possible to get a completely independent panel to conduct tests and announce results?

comments.text:
So I usually don’t comment on videos, and I say this with utmost respect for the passion that you have for the AI space Wes, but to give constructive feedback: given that you put out a large quantity of videos in a short period of time, and each of these videos have pretty clickbaity titles and thumbnails, the actual content of each video feels like it’s falling short of the claims made in the titles/thumbnails. 

Maybe I’m not the target audience here (I’m a creative who is fascinated with AI but am nowhere close to a software engineer, not sure if that’s who these are for) but as someone who is genuinely fascinated by the AI space and where everything is headed, I feel that these videos should be less frequent and contain less speculation and conjecture. A lot of your videos lately have been just reading off other people’s tweets saying “this guy in the AI space said this, whereas this guy in the AI space said that”, but none of it feels to have any substance. If you’re going to put out videos, I feel that these content you’re covering should be less speculative, less of just reading off people’s tweets and and less of saying “maybe this will happen, these people say maybe that will happen, but nobody is necessarily certain or correct”. 

It just doesn’t feel very productive, and I feel that if you’re going to put a video out, they should be based off of more significant milestones that are actually world-changing and have more impact on the average person, rather than breaking it down bit by bit every single day and speculating on what might happen. Just my take, and just trying to help. Cheers
